summary: A guide to using the Simple Network Management Protocol for configuration management, not just monitoring. It is aimed at vendors who build network devices, application developers, and the operators who manage networks. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3512 is a guide to using SNMP to change how a network device is set up, rather than only to read what it is doing. It covers how to group configuration changes so that they happen together or not at all, how to tell when a change has actually taken effect, how to report what changed, and how to send the same settings to many devices with less traffic.

subtitle: Current practice for using SNMP to configure network devices, not only to monitor them

tldr.problem: SNMP was built for monitoring, but networks now need a standard way to change how a device is configured, and the change has to be applied completely or not at all, verified, and kept consistent across many devices.
tldr.mechanism: The document collects the practices that work: transaction control in the MIB modules, RowStatus and separate administrative and operational objects for activation, notifications that report what changed, and template objects that let one set of defaults cover many instances.
tldr.outcome: It is a guidance document rather than a specification. It tells vendors, application developers and operators how to design and use SNMP for configuration, and it is emphatic that SNMPv3 should be used for it.

facts.label: Transaction control objects
facts.value: RowStatus, explicit activate objects, multi-level defaults

facts.label: Notification rate limit example
facts.value: No more than one message every 60 seconds

today: RFC 3512 is an Informational memo published in April 2003, produced by the SNMPCONF Working Group, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is guidance rather than a specification: it defines no protocol and no new objects, and it points at the MIB modules and standards that carry the mechanisms it describes.

sections.title: Why Configure Networks with SNMP
sections.content:
RFC 3512 is a guide to using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) for configuration management, not only monitoring. It is written for the vendors who build network elements, the developers of management applications, and the people who acquire and deploy the technology in their networks.

The Internet Standard Management Framework that SNMP belongs to has five parts: the overall architecture in RFC 3411; the mechanisms for describing and naming management objects, SMIv1 and SMIv2; the message protocols SNMPv1, SNMPv2c and SNMPv3; the protocol operations for accessing management information; and a set of fundamental applications together with the view-based access control model. Managed objects are reached through a virtual store called the Management Information Base, or MIB, and the objects in it are defined using the SMI.

The document's starting point is that configuration has changed. Networks have grown in scale, with more and larger devices, in functionality, and in rate of change: a configuration can no longer be assumed to be specified once and updated rarely. Correct configuration is a prerequisite for deploying the services that earn money, and the growth in size and complexity increases the need for a standard configuration mechanism that is tightly integrated with the performance and fault management systems.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains how to use SNMP to change how a device is set up, not just to read what it is doing. It is written for the people who build devices, write the management software, and run the network.

sections.title: Transactions and Verification
sections.content:
Configuration activity causes one or more state changes in an element, and it often takes an arbitrary number of commands and amount of data to make up a change. The configuration system should treat the overall change atomically so that the number of states the element passes through is minimised: the goal is for a change request either to be completely executed or not at all. The document calls this transactional integrity, and it is what makes it possible to build reliable configuration systems that keep track of an element's overall state and work in the presence of error states.

Five features are required of a well-designed configuration system. It must offer transaction control at many levels of granularity, from an entire configuration down to one attribute. It must understand multi-level defaulting, so that a command can carry a set of defaults for instances that meet certain criteria instead of setting each instance separately. It must allow flexibility in what counts as a successful transaction, which cannot be decided at the protocol level alone. It must support time-indexed transaction control, so that transactions and their completion status are reported by the managed elements and stored in a repository that can record who made the change even if the change was not carried out by the system recording it. And it must support transactional security, so that a request is accepted or denied according to the security policy in force in the managed element.

Verification is the other half of the job. The document describes a change management procedure of pre-test, change and re-test: verify that the system is presently working properly, make the changes and wait for convergence, then verify once again. Networks and devices under SNMP support this readily, because SNMP provides integrated monitoring, configuration and diagnostic capabilities, and the key is the sequencing of the protocol operations. The example given is a pair of OSPF timers set to the same value, which leaves two routers forming an adjacency and then cycling in and out of it, never reaching a stable state; with the procedure in place that would have been discovered without touching the production network.
sections.plainLanguage: A configuration change should either happen completely or not at all, so that the device passes through as few intermediate states as possible. The document also insists on checking the device before and after the change, because a change that looks successful can still leave the network unstable.

sections.title: Designing Configuration MIB Modules
sections.content:
The document's longest section is about designing the MIB modules that hold configuration. It starts with the criteria that the widely deployed BRIDGE-MIB of RFC 1493 used: start with a small set of essential objects and add only as needed; require objects to be essential for fault or configuration management; consider evidence of current use; limit the total number of objects; exclude objects that are simply derivable from others; and avoid instrumenting critical sections heavily. Eight years of further experience added four more, among them identifying the goals of the module before designing it, treating usability rather than the object count as the goal, supporting explicit error state, capability and capacity objects, and defining derived objects when they would reduce the complexity of a management application.

Rows of a table are where configuration lives, and the RowStatus textual convention is the standard way to control them. A RowStatus column holds the state of a conceptual row and controls its creation, deletion, activation and deactivation; setting it to active makes the row committed. The document warns that RowStatus should not be used to control the activation of configuration, because an agent may remove a row that has been in the notInService state for an abnormally long time, and it recommends separate administrative and operational objects instead, where the administrative object holds what was asked for and the operational object reports what the subsystem has actually done.

Several further practices are recommended. Fate sharing between related tables should be defined explicitly, so that deleting a row in one table deletes the matching row in the other, and the document gives the sparse relationship between the bridge and interface tables as a case where the answer has to be written down. A transaction control object can be a scalar that commits everything pending when set to a particular value. Creating a row should use the notReady state while the required columnar values are still missing, and a row that fits inside one SET PDU can be created with createAndGo in the same operation. For state tracking, a module can expose the number of rows in a table, a timestamp of the last change, or notifications that carry the changed columns. Where configuration data is large, three design options are offered: partitioning the data with multiple indices or several tables, time-based indexing, and a control MIB module that manages a separate data delivery protocol.

The agent side matters as well. The document argues for idempotency, which means that repeating the same set operation results in a single activation, because SNMP runs over UDP and a lost response makes the manager send the request again. The MIB document is a contract between the management application and the agent, and the agent also has to manage the state of a subsystem that is being reconfigured underneath it.
sections.plainLanguage: Configuration lives in table rows, and a standard column called RowStatus controls what happens to a row. The document warns against using that column to switch configuration on, and asks for one object that records what was asked for and another that reports what actually happened.

sections.title: Setting Configuration and Activating It
sections.content:
Two ideas are separated here: the setting of configuration objects and the activation of those changes in the actual subsystem. It often only makes sense to activate a group of objects as a single transaction. The document suggests that a complex configuration has a master on/off switch as well as strategically placed switches that partition the activation, so that a series of set operations installs the configuration without making the agent activate each object as it arrives, which would introduce operational instability with every changed object instance.

The same separation shows up in the objects themselves. A table can expose a columnar object that is strictly for administrative control, whose value reflects the last set or defaulted value, and a companion read-only object that gives the current state of activation or deactivation. The two may differ for a period of activation latency, and that is why they are separate. The DISMAN-SCHEDULE-MIB is used as the example, with schedAdminStatus holding the desired state and schedOperStatus reporting the operational state. Persistence is treated the same way: many devices have two levels of it, data that is persistent only until changed or until the system is reinitialised, and data made permanent as part of accepting the configuration, and some MIB objects carry both a StorageType value and a description of the behaviour.

Latency is the reason this matters. A set operation may be answered before the subsystem has accepted and installed the configuration, so the agent should process the change as soon as the Set PDU has been processed and then update the status objects when the save to persistent storage and the activation have succeeded, or send a notification that the operation is complete. A single object type used both to control and to report on state can produce confusing and paradoxical results, and the document's example is a wheel that has been told to spin counter-clockwise but is still slowing down towards the idle state when it is read back.

Notifications carry the change information and the errors. The document recommends SNMPv3 for configuration operations because of its security capabilities, and InformRequest PDUs in preference to TRAP PDUs, because the recipient answers with a Response PDU and the agent then knows whether it needs to retransmit. A notification that reports configuration changes should say who made the change, using the transport address and SNMP parameters of the command generator where possible. Notifications should be limited, either by describing situations in which they need not be sent, by a temporal limit such as no more than one message every 60 seconds, or by a fixed limit on the number of messages sent. The SNMP protocol error mechanisms should not be relied on alone to report application level errors, because they rarely say whether a request failed for a resource reason, a security reason, or an application error.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing a value to a device is not the same as the device acting on it. The document asks for separate objects for the two, so that a manager can see when a change has actually taken effect, and for notifications that say what changed and who changed it.

sections.title: Policy-Based Management and Templates
sections.content:
The last large part of the document is about policy-based management, which grew out of the same problem: configuration data kept multiplying. The term policy has been used loosely, and the document gives it a specific meaning here, with three properties defining a policy-based configuration system.

First, default configuration data can be specified for a number of instances of managed elements, where those instances can be correlated in a data-driven or algorithmic way, and the engine that does the correlation and activates the instances may sit in the agent or outside it. Where the representation of these defaults is in the MIB design itself, the object types supporting this notion are called template objects. Second, the activation of instance data derived from those template objects results from minimal activation directives from the management application, once the template instances have been established. Third, somewhat independently, the architecture of the agent may accommodate the definition and evaluation of management and configuration policies, and the side effects of that evaluation typically include the activation of configuration directives.

The motivation is scale. An agent implementing the Bridge MIB could represent a large VLAN with some 65,000 port entries, and configuring it would mean creating rows in dot1dStpPortTable and dot1DStaticTable for each virtual port, each with several parameters. Setting each instance individually is how configuration is done today, with file transfer, individual MIB objects, or many CLI commands, and in each approach the details for every instance are repeated. Template-based data organisation abstracts the details above the instance level, which means fewer SET requests are sent to a managed device. A scalable policy system also needs to layer the application of defaults at discrete ranges of granularity, from the breadth of a network service down to instance-level data.

The document also lists the information a policy system needs to make good decisions, among them the operational state of the elements to be configured, whether the sub-components are available for use, and the capabilities of the devices in the network. It separates distribution of a policy, activation of a policy, and the changes or failures that happen while a policy is expected to be active: an interface that is down and covered by a policy that is not scheduled for activation until later is not an error at all.
sections.plainLanguage: The document's answer to large configurations is templates. A template holds the settings that apply to many instances at once, so the manager sends a few instructions rather than thousands, and the agent works out which instances each one covers.

sections.title: Deployment and Security Issues
sections.content:
The deployment section starts with three assumptions about real configuration systems. Operations must understand and be trained in the technology, because no configuration system can prevent an untrained operator from causing outages. Systems undergoing change must cope with the unexpected loss of communication at any time, so the network element has to leave the configuration in a consistent or recognisable state, either by rolling back to a previously valid state or by changing to a well-defined or default state. And configuration exists on a scale from set and forget to near real-time change control, so the design has to take the expected rate and volume of change into account.

On security the recommendation is plain. Vendors should not ship a device with a community string of public or private, and agents should not define default community strings except where they are needed to bootstrap devices that have no secondary management interface. SNMPv3 is recommended for all network management applications, because it provides authorization, authentication and confidentiality protection, and it is essential for any device that supports SNMP-based configuration. The default state of the RFC 1215 authentication notifications should be off, because sending authentication failure information by itself can be a security liability, and traps that carry a community string can leak it to anyone on shared links.

Sensitive objects need care. MIB modules that hold keys, passwords or other sensitive data must say how that data should be protected, and even where a device supports DES, configuring keys for other protocols over SNMP sets protected by DES should not be allowed when those keys are longer than the 56 bit DES key protecting the SNMP transmission. Confidentiality is not a mandatory part of the SNMPv3 management framework, so the document recommends that new MIB modules indicate the level of security appropriate to their object types, and that object grouping be designed with view-based access control in mind so that users can scope what a given user and view can see. The security considerations section at the end of the document reiterates the SNMPv3 recommendation and the need to authenticate the management entities that start a configuration change and to protect the integrity of the configuration data itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The document's security advice is to use SNMPv3 and to change the default community strings, which have been widely known and exploited. It also warns that objects holding passwords need their own protection, because SNMPv3 does not make confidentiality mandatory.

messages.label: Pre-test GET
messages.note: Read the stability counter to see that the system is working.

messages.label: Wait for convergence
messages.note: Give the device time to settle.

messages.label: Re-test GET
messages.note: Read the same counter again and compare it with the first reading.

viz.caption: THE ROWSTATUS VALUES A CONFIGURATION TABLE USES

items.label: active
items.desc: The conceptual row is available for use by the managed device.

items.label: notInService
items.desc: The row exists but is not in service. The agent must remove rows left in this state for an abnormally long period.

items.label: notReady
items.desc: The row cannot be activated yet because the required columnar values are not set.

items.label: createAndGo
items.desc: Creates the row and makes it active in the same operation.

items.label: createAndWait
items.desc: Creates the row without activating it, so the rest of the row can be filled in first.

viz.caption: THE THREE PROPERTIES OF POLICY-BASED CONFIGURATION

items.title: Defaults at the template level
items.text: Default configuration data can be specified for many instances, correlated in a data-driven or algorithmic way. The engine may sit in the agent or outside it.

items.title: Minimal activation
items.text: Instance data derived from a template is activated by minimal directives from the management application, once the template instances exist.

items.title: Policy evaluation
items.text: The agent may hold and evaluate policies, and the side effects of that evaluation typically include activating configuration directives.
